title: Why Qualified Custody Is the Safer Way to Hold Bitcoin
summary: If you own bitcoin, the real question isn't if someone can hack your wallet. It's "what happens if the device itself has a hidden flaw I could never have caught?"
body_markdown:
If you own bitcoin, the real question isn't if someone can hack your wallet. It's "what happens if the device itself has a hidden flaw I could never have caught?"


In July 2026, that exact scenario played out. A bug hidden in a popular hardware wallet let hackers drain about 1,816 BTC (~$116 million) from more than 5,000 wallets. The owners hadn't made a mistake. The flaw was built into the device, and there was no way for an everyday user to spot it.


That's the tradeoff with holding your own keys. You're in full control, but you're also fully responsible, for your own mistakes and for any flaw in the hardware or software you're trusting.


## A different kind of protection


Qualified custody works differently. Instead of one device holding everything, a regulated custodian holds your assets, with a legal duty to protect them, rather than relying solely on software you use yourself. At BitGo, that means:


-


Your assets are segregated from BitGo's own money and from other clients' funds.


-


Moving funds requires sign-off from multiple authorized parties or keys, making it much more difficult for bad actors to wipe out your account


-


Your assets are insured[up to $250 million](https://www.bitgo.com/solutions/insurance/) against loss, theft, or misuse (subject to policy terms).


-


BitGo has protected billions in crypto for more than a decade with a strong track record of operational security.


None of this means holding your own keys is a bad idea for everyone. But the more your holdings are worth, the more it helps to have more than one line of defense, and someone legally on the hook to protect you.
